entries.name: Antifragility
entries.oneLiner: Some things gain from disorder — beyond robust, they get stronger when stressed, exposed, or shocked.
entries.description: Nassim Nicholas Taleb's term for systems that benefit from volatility, errors, and stressors — the opposite of fragile, with 'robust' as the neutral midpoint. Bones, immune systems, evolution, restaurant industries, and barbell investment portfolios are antifragile because their downside is bounded while upside compounds with shocks. The asymmetry — convex payoff to randomness — is the technical core. Crucially, fragility/antifragility is a property of the response curve, not the event: you can detect it before the rare shock arrives.
entries.example: Muscles and bones strengthen under load and atrophy without it (Wolff's law). Startup ecosystems are antifragile — individual startups die, but the system learns from each failure. A barbell portfolio (90% T-bills + 10% venture bets) loses little in crashes and captures upside in booms.
entries.howToApply: For any plan, ask: 'If a 3-sigma shock hits this, do I lose more than I gain, or gain more than I lose?' Engineer asymmetry: cap downside (small bets, stop-losses, optionality) while leaving upside uncapped. Add small, frequent stressors to systems you want to strengthen — fasting, code chaos engineering, public speaking reps. Avoid debt and just-in-time supply chains where shocks compound losses.
entries.pitfalls: Antifragility is a property of payoff structure, not a vibe. Calling yourself 'antifragile' because you survived a hard year is just robustness. Also, exposing a fragile system (a child, a relationship) to stressors hoping they'll toughen up can simply break them.
entries.origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder, 2012.

entries.name: Beginner's Mind (Shoshin)
entries.oneLiner: In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities; in the expert's there are few.
entries.description: Shoshin (初心) is a Zen concept of approaching any subject — even one you know — with the openness, eagerness, and lack of preconception of a beginner. Shunryū Suzuki popularized it for the West in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (1970): 'In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert's mind there are few.' The idea traces to Dōgen (13th c., Shōbōgenzō) and the related proverb 'shoshin wasuru bekarazu' (never forget the beginner's mind), coined by Zeami in 1424.
entries.example: Tech: Andy Grove's 'only the paranoid survive' — Intel survived by repeatedly forgetting it was Intel. Sports: Roger Federer overhauling his backhand at 35 with a coach treating him like a junior. Daily: a senior doctor asking the medical student 'what would you do?' before answering, and learning something.
entries.howToApply: When you catch yourself thinking 'I already know this,' ask three beginner questions: 'What would I see if I'd never seen this before? What is the dumbest possible question? What would I do if I had to teach it to a 12-year-old?' Once a quarter, take a real lesson in something you're 'expert' at — the gap between confidence and competence usually surprises.
entries.pitfalls: Confused with false modesty or refusing to use hard-won expertise. In high-stakes domains (surgery, aviation), beginner's-mind bravado kills — checklists and accumulated tacit knowledge exist for reasons. Use shoshin for openness to new evidence, not as an excuse to ignore protocols.
entries.origin: Zen Buddhist tradition; Dōgen, Shōbōgenzō (13th century); phrase 'shoshin wasuru bekarazu' from Zeami Motokiyo (1424); popularized by Shunryū Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (1970).

entries.name: Black Swan
entries.oneLiner: Rare, high-impact events that are unpredictable in advance but rationalized as obvious afterward — and they dominate history.
entries.description: Taleb's Black Swan has three properties: (1) it lies outside regular expectations because nothing in the past convincingly points to it, (2) it carries extreme impact, and (3) human nature concocts post-hoc explanations making it appear predictable. Most of the variance in long-run outcomes — 9/11, COVID-19, the printing press, the internet, your spouse — comes from Black Swans, yet our tools (Gaussian statistics, base-rate forecasting) systematically underweight them. The error isn't bad prediction; it's predicting at all in domains ruled by extremes ('Extremistan').
entries.example: Long-Term Capital Management's 1998 collapse: models built on 5 years of data assumed Russian sovereign default was a 1-in-many-billion event. COVID-19 pandemic response in February 2020. The 2007 publication of the iPhone reshaping a decade of business models nobody plotted on a 2006 spreadsheet.
entries.howToApply: Stop trying to predict Black Swans; prepare for them. Distinguish 'Mediocristan' domains (heights, calorie intake — Gaussian, safe to forecast) from 'Extremistan' (wealth, virality, casualties — fat-tailed). In Extremistan, focus on exposure: minimize fragility to negative shocks (insurance, redundancy, low debt) and maximize exposure to positive ones (small bets on many long-shots). Treat any forecast beyond 12 months in Extremistan as entertainment.
entries.pitfalls: The label is overused — every surprise gets called a Black Swan, including events that were forecasted and ignored ('grey swans' or 'white swans' in Taleb's language). Also, hindsight bias makes past Black Swans look obviously predictable, creating the illusion that next time will be different.
entries.origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable, 2007 (drawing on Hume and Popper on the problem of induction).

entries.name: Bloom's Taxonomy
entries.oneLiner: Learning has levels — remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create — and most studying stops at the bottom two.
entries.description: Bloom's framework classifies cognitive tasks by depth. Lower levels (recall, comprehension) are necessary but insufficient: most exam failures and on-the-job stumbles happen at the higher tiers (apply a concept to a novel case, evaluate competing options, design something new). The 2001 Anderson-Krathwohl revision flipped the top two so 'create' sits above 'evaluate' and turned the nouns into verbs.
entries.example: A student can recite the definition of opportunity cost (remember) and explain it in their own words (understand) but freezes when asked to evaluate whether to take a job offer using it (apply/evaluate). The gap reveals where studying stopped.
entries.howToApply: 1) For any topic, write one question per Bloom level and try to answer all six. 2) Push study sessions past 'I can define it' to 'I can use it to solve a new problem'. 3) When teaching or designing curricula, label tasks by level and ensure the assessment matches the goal. 4) For interview prep, expect questions at apply/analyze/evaluate, not just recall.
entries.pitfalls: The hierarchy is a useful heuristic, not a strict cognitive ladder; real tasks blend levels (analysis often requires creation). Treating it as a rigid sequence can delay meaningful work. Empirical support for the strict ordering is weaker than the framework's ubiquity in education suggests.
entries.origin: Benjamin Bloom et al., 'Taxonomy of Educational Objectives' (1956); revised by Anderson & Krathwohl (2001).

entries.name: Chesterton's Fence
entries.oneLiner: Don't remove a rule, fence, or piece of code until you understand why it was put there in the first place.
entries.description: Chesterton's principle says that before tearing down an existing institution or constraint, you should be able to explain its original purpose. If you can't, you're not yet qualified to remove it — because you don't yet understand the system. It's a conservative bias against overconfident reform.
entries.example: A new tech lead deletes a 'weird' retry-with-jitter wrapper around an API call because it looks redundant. The next morning, the downstream service rate-limits everyone and the on-call pager melts. The wrapper existed for a reason that wasn't documented.
entries.howToApply: Before deleting any rule, config flag, comment, line of code, or process: (1) Find the commit/email/policy that introduced it. (2) Ask the longest-tenured person what failure it prevented. (3) Write down the failure mode in one sentence. (4) Then decide whether the failure mode still applies. If it does, leave the fence.
entries.pitfalls: Used dogmatically, it ossifies dead bureaucracy — sometimes the original reason genuinely no longer applies (legacy compliance, deprecated dependencies). The principle says understand-before-removing, not never-remove. Also, some fences were built by people who themselves didn't know why; don't venerate cargo cult.
entries.origin: G. K. Chesterton, 1929, in 'The Thing: Why I Am a Catholic,' chapter 'The Drift from Domesticity.'

entries.name: Emergence
entries.oneLiner: Higher-level properties — consciousness, traffic jams, market prices — arise from interactions between parts and cannot be predicted from the parts alone.
entries.description: Emergence describes how simple local rules produce surprising global behavior: water is wet but H2O molecules aren't; a flock has shape but no bird does; markets clear without any agent setting the price. Weak emergence is in-principle reducible to the parts (in practice intractable); strong emergence claims genuinely novel causal powers at higher levels and is philosophically contested. The practical takeaway: studying components in isolation can miss the phenomenon entirely.
entries.example: Conway's Game of Life: four trivial rules generate gliders, oscillators, and Turing-complete computation. Or: no single ant is intelligent, but the colony solves shortest-path foraging problems. Or: city-level traffic patterns that no driver intends.
entries.howToApply: When debugging a team, market, or product, ask whether the issue lives at the interaction layer rather than the individual layer. Replace 'who is the bad actor?' with 'what local rules and incentives are people responding to?' For design, set simple rules and incentives and let behavior emerge, rather than micromanaging outcomes.
entries.pitfalls: Treating 'emergence' as a magic word that explains anything ('consciousness just emerges') is empty. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes the strong/weak distinction is genuinely disputed. Also, emergent behavior can be malign (bank runs, mob violence) — 'emergent' is not a synonym for 'good.'
entries.origin: G. H. Lewes coined the term in Problems of Life and Mind, 1875; modern treatment in complexity science (Santa Fe Institute, 1980s+).

entries.name: Emotional Bank Account
entries.oneLiner: Trust in a relationship behaves like a bank balance: small deposits compound, withdrawals cost more than they seem.
entries.description: Stephen Covey's metaphor in Habit 5 of 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People.' Every interaction is a deposit (kept promises, kindness, listening, apologies, integrity) or a withdrawal (broken promises, criticism, dishonesty, taking for granted). A high balance lets the relationship absorb mistakes and hard conversations; a low balance means even small slights overdraw the account. Covey lists six major deposits, including understanding the individual, attending to little things, keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, showing personal integrity, and apologizing sincerely.
entries.example: You've been late to dinners three weeks running (withdrawals). When you finally raise a sensitive concern about money, your partner reacts sharply—not because the concern is unfair but because the account is overdrawn.
entries.howToApply: 1) Make one deliberate deposit daily: a thank-you, a kept micro-promise, a remembered detail. 2) Before a hard conversation, check the balance—if low, deposit first. 3) When you withdraw, apologize specifically and quickly—delayed apologies depreciate. 4) Track patterns: which behaviors does your partner experience as deposits vs withdrawals? They're not always what you'd predict.
entries.pitfalls: It's a metaphor, not a transaction—'I did three nice things, you owe me' is keeping score, which itself is a withdrawal. Deposits in your currency may not register in theirs (links to love-languages caveat). The model can let chronic harmers paper over real damage with small kindnesses; some withdrawals (betrayal, abuse) can't be offset by deposits.
entries.origin: Stephen R. Covey, 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People,' Free Press, 1989.

entries.name: Feedback Loops
entries.oneLiner: Outputs that become inputs — reinforcing loops amplify change, balancing loops resist it; both shape almost every outcome over time.
entries.description: A feedback loop exists whenever the result of a process feeds back to influence the process itself. Reinforcing (positive) loops produce exponential growth or collapse: compound interest, viral spread, runaway anxiety. Balancing (negative) loops seek a target: thermostats, hunger, market prices. Most real systems are tangles of both, with delays that cause oscillation and overshoot. Recognizing the loop type predicts whether a trend will accelerate, stabilize, or oscillate.
entries.example: Compound interest is a reinforcing loop on wealth; credit-card debt is the same loop running against you. A workout habit creates a reinforcing loop (energy -> more workouts -> more energy) until injury introduces a balancing loop. Social-media engagement algorithms are reinforcing loops on outrage.
entries.howToApply: For any goal, ask: 'What reinforcing loop, once started, would make this easier each week?' Then engineer a tiny first turn of that loop (post one thing, save one dollar, run one mile). For problems, ask: 'What balancing loop is fighting me?' (homeostasis, organizational antibodies) and design around it rather than through it.
entries.pitfalls: Calling everything a 'feedback loop' adds zero precision. The useful version specifies the variables, the polarity, and the delay. Also, reinforcing loops in your favor have natural limits — exponential growth always hits a balancing constraint eventually.
entries.origin: Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics, 1948; formalized in system dynamics by Forrester and Meadows.

entries.name: First-Principles Thinking
entries.oneLiner: Break a problem down to its fundamental, undeniable truths and reason upward from there instead of arguing by analogy.
entries.description: First-principles reasoning means decomposing a belief or problem until you hit foundational facts that cannot be deduced from anything more basic, then rebuilding your conclusion from those atoms. It is the opposite of reasoning by analogy ('we do it this way because everyone does'). The discipline forces you to surface assumptions you didn't know you were making and exposes inherited 'common sense' that no longer holds.
entries.example: Elon Musk famously priced rocket components by raw material cost (aluminum, copper, carbon fiber) instead of accepting industry quotes, concluding SpaceX could build for ~2% of the prevailing price. Same pattern: a startup challenging a $20k MRI by costing the magnet, coil, and compute separately.
entries.howToApply: Pick a belief you act on weekly ('I need a degree to switch fields'). Write it down. List every assumption beneath it. For each, ask: 'Is this a law of physics, a law of economics, or a social convention?' Discard convention-level assumptions and rebuild the plan using only the hard constraints. Use the '5 Whys' as a forcing function.
entries.pitfalls: Easy to mistake confident contrarianism for first-principles thinking. Reasoning from scratch is expensive — for routine decisions, analogy is faster and usually correct. Also, 'fundamentals' you derive may themselves be assumptions; physicists revise theirs every century.
entries.origin: Aristotle (4th century BCE, Posterior Analytics — 'archai'); revived in modern strategy by Charlie Munger and popularized by Elon Musk.

entries.name: Friction (Make Good Things Easy)
entries.oneLiner: Behavior follows the path of least resistance, so reduce friction for what you want and add friction to what you don't.
entries.description: A robust finding across behavioral science: small changes in the cost of an action — seconds saved, clicks avoided, distance shortened — produce large changes in behavior, often dwarfing the effect of motivation or information. The mirror principle is that adding even trivial friction (a password, a 10-minute delay, putting the phone in another room) substantially reduces unwanted behavior. This is the practical engine behind Thaler's 'choice architecture' and Clear's 'environment design.'
entries.example: Logging out of Twitter and deleting the app from your phone, so checking it requires opening a laptop and typing a password, can cut usage by an order of magnitude — not because your willpower changed but because the cost did. Conversely, leaving running shoes by the door makes a morning run measurably more likely.
entries.howToApply: 1) For one habit you want, list every step from cue to completion and remove or shorten as many as possible (gym clothes laid out the night before, meal prepped Sunday). 2) For one habit you want less of, add at least 20 seconds of friction (delete the app, use a website blocker, give the credit card to a partner). 3) Re-engineer the environment, not yourself.
entries.pitfalls: Friction is undermined by determined motivation — if you really want it, you will route around it — so it works best for weakly held habits. Excessive friction on good behavior (overly elaborate productivity systems) becomes its own obstacle. And adding friction to others' behavior can become coercive.
entries.origin: Synthesized from Kurt Lewin's force-field analysis (1940s), Thaler and Sunstein's Nudge (2008), and BJ Fogg's Behavior Model (2009); popularized in habits literature by James Clear.

entries.name: Goodhart's Law
entries.oneLiner: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
entries.description: Optimizing for a proxy metric tends to corrupt the metric and the underlying goal it was meant to track. People game the score, the score and the goal decouple, and outcomes worsen even as the dashboard improves. The pithier rephrasing is by Marilyn Strathern (1997); the underlying point generalizes Campbell's Law in social science.
entries.example: When Wells Fargo set aggressive cross-sell targets per banker, employees opened ~3.5 million unauthorized accounts (2016). The metric ('accounts per customer') skyrocketed while the goal ('customer relationships') collapsed.
entries.howToApply: Pair every quantitative target with a counter-metric that catches gaming (e.g., sales volume + customer-retention rate). Rotate metrics, audit randomly, and ask employees what they'd do to game each KPI before launching it. Prefer multiple imperfect indicators over one perfect-looking one.
entries.pitfalls: Doesn't mean metrics are useless—just that single targets are fragile. Some critics overuse it to dismiss any measurement; the fix is better incentive design, not no measurement.
entries.origin: Charles Goodhart, Bank of England economist, 'Problems of Monetary Management' (1975); popularized phrasing by Marilyn Strathern (1997).

entries.name: Hanlon's Razor
entries.oneLiner: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by stupidity, incompetence, or ordinary human carelessness.
entries.description: Hanlon's Razor is a heuristic against paranoid attribution. When someone's action harms you, the prior probability of incompetence, miscommunication, or distraction is usually much higher than coordinated malice. It nudges you toward charitable explanations — and, crucially, toward responses (clarify, ask) that work for both cases.
entries.example: Your manager doesn't reply to your raise email for a week. Malice-frame: she's stalling to avoid you. Hanlon-frame: she has 400 unread messages and forgot. You send a one-line nudge instead of stewing — and she replies in ten minutes, apologizing.
entries.howToApply: When you feel wronged, write two columns: 'malice explanation' and 'mundane explanation' (overload, unclear instructions, tired, no context). If the mundane column is plausible, take the action that fits both worlds — usually a clarifying question. Reserve malice-attributions for repeated, specific patterns with clear motive.
entries.pitfalls: Overapplied, it becomes a shield for actual bad actors ('he's not racist, he's just clueless'). Patterns matter: one missed email is incompetence, twelve is a signal. Also, in high-stakes adversarial environments (security, negotiations), assuming incompetence can be costly. Sometimes it really is malice.
entries.origin: Robert J. Hanlon, 1980, in a submission to 'Murphy's Law Book Two.' Similar formulations appear earlier in Goethe and in Heinlein's 1941 novella 'Logic of Empire' ('You have attributed conditions to villainy that simply result from stupidity').

entries.name: Hormesis
entries.oneLiner: Living systems get stronger from controlled doses of the stressors that, in larger doses, would harm them.
entries.description: Hormesis describes a biphasic dose-response: low-to-moderate exposure to a stressor triggers adaptive responses that exceed baseline, while high doses cause harm. Edward Calabrese's reviews (Calabrese & Baldwin, *Nature* 2003; *Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology*, 2004) documented over 600 substances showing this U-shape. The framework unifies why exercise (mechanical and metabolic stress), heat and cold exposure (HSP induction, brown-fat activation), caloric restriction and fasting (autophagy, AMPK signaling), and even phytochemicals (sulforaphane via Nrf2) confer benefits — they trigger the cell's own defense machinery (Mattson, *Ageing Research Reviews*, 2008).
entries.example: Someone who progressively works up to a weekly 20-minute 80°C sauna session shows improved cardiovascular markers comparable to moderate exercise (Laukkanen et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015 Finnish cohort) — yet a single 90-minute extreme session causes heat stroke. Same input, opposite outcomes, depending on dose.
entries.howToApply: 1) Pick one or two hormetic stressors and progress gradually: lifting (load), Zone 2/intervals (volume), sauna (heat duration), cold plunge (time and temperature), time-restricted eating (window length). 2) Recover deliberately — adaptation happens in the rest, not the stress. 3) Stack stressors carefully; high training load plus a calorie deficit plus poor sleep is a path to injury, not adaptation. 4) Track a baseline marker (resting HR, lift weight, sleep quality) and stop progressing if it gets worse for two weeks.
entries.pitfalls: Hormesis is dose-dependent; 'if some is good, more is better' is exactly wrong. Vulnerable populations (pregnancy, cardiac disease, elderly with frailty) need medical guidance for cold and heat. Some claims marketed as 'hormetic' (microdosing toxins, extreme fasts) lack evidence. Calabrese has been criticized for industry funding ties that complicate his policy positions on chemical exposures, though the biological phenomenon itself is well-established.
entries.origin: The term 'hormesis' was coined by Southam & Ehrlich, 1943; modern revival and quantitative framework: Edward Calabrese & Linda Baldwin, *Nature* and *Toxicological Sciences*, 2002–2003; Mark Mattson's neurohormesis work, NIH, 2000s.

entries.name: Identity-Based Habits
entries.oneLiner: Lasting habits form when the behavior becomes evidence for who you are, not a chore in pursuit of an outcome.
entries.description: James Clear's framing distinguishes outcome-based change ('I want to lose 20 pounds'), process-based change ('I'll go to the gym 3x a week'), and identity-based change ('I am the kind of person who doesn't miss workouts'). The claim, supported by research on self-concept and behavior consistency (e.g., Christopher Bryan's work showing 'be a voter' beats 'go vote' in turnout experiments), is that identity creates self-reinforcing motivation: the behavior is no longer in tension with who you are.
entries.example: A smoker offered a cigarette who says 'No thanks, I'm trying to quit' is still a smoker negotiating with each offer. One who says 'No thanks, I'm not a smoker' has reframed the choice as identity-consistent — Clear cites this distinction directly, and it tracks with longitudinal quitting research.
entries.howToApply: 1) For each goal, write the identity behind it: not 'run a marathon' but 'I am a runner.' 2) Pick the smallest behavior that is evidence for that identity and do it daily ('a runner runs, even one block'). 3) Use language carefully — 'I don't' beats 'I can't' in self-control studies (Patrick & Hagtvedt, 2012). 4) Surround yourself with people for whom the identity is normal.
entries.pitfalls: Identity claims without behavior become posturing, and rigid identities can backfire when you slip ('I'm a runner who skipped → I'm a fraud → I quit'). Useful identities are flexible and grounded in repeated action, not declared once and defended.
entries.origin: Framing popularized by James Clear in Atomic Habits (2018); empirical roots in Bryan, Walton, Rogers & Dweck's voter studies (PNAS, 2011) and Patrick & Hagtvedt's 'I don't vs. I can't' research (Journal of Consumer Research, 2012).

entries.name: Inversion (Invert, Always Invert)
entries.oneLiner: Solve problems backwards by asking what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things.
entries.description: Inversion flips a goal on its head: instead of asking 'how do I succeed?', ask 'what would cause catastrophic failure here?' and systematically eliminate those paths. Munger argues many hard forward problems become tractable when inverted. It pairs well with checklists because failure modes are often more concrete and enumerable than success recipes.
entries.example: Instead of 'how do I have a happy marriage?', ask 'what reliably destroys marriages?' (contempt, financial deceit, neglect) and remove those. Instead of 'how do I get rich?', ask 'how do people go broke?' (leverage, single-stock concentration, lifestyle creep) and avoid them.
entries.howToApply: For any goal, write a second column titled 'How would I guarantee the opposite?'. List 5-10 failure paths, then convert each into a 'do-not-do' rule. Run a quarterly 'how would I sabotage this project?' session before strategy planning.
entries.pitfalls: Inversion identifies what to avoid but not what to pursue — used alone it produces risk-averse, uncreative strategies. Avoidance lists can also become superstition (avoiding things merely correlated with failure). Combine with forward thinking, not as a substitute.
entries.origin: Borrowed by Charlie Munger (Berkshire Hathaway, 1990s-2000s talks, esp. 'A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom,' 1994) from 19th-century mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi's dictum 'man muss immer umkehren' (invert, always invert).

entries.name: Ladder of Inference
entries.oneLiner: We climb from observable data to conclusions through invisible rungs of selection, interpretation, and assumption — and forget we climbed.
entries.description: The Ladder of Inference describes the rapid, unconscious cognitive steps from raw observation to belief and action: we select data, add meaning, make assumptions, draw conclusions, adopt beliefs, and take actions — each rung selecting and discarding information. Conflicts often happen because two people climb different ladders from the same data and argue at the top.
entries.example: In a meeting, Priya doesn't speak up about your proposal. You climb the ladder: she's quiet → she disagrees → she thinks it's bad → she doesn't respect my judgment → I'll exclude her next time. Actually she had a migraine. The disagreement you 'remember' was constructed in your head in 0.4 seconds.
entries.howToApply: When you feel a strong reaction to someone's behavior: (1) Name the observable data (what was actually said/done, video-camera level). (2) Note the meaning you added. (3) Note the assumption that bridged data and meaning. (4) Ask the other person about one rung: 'You went quiet — what was going on?' Test the ladder, don't defend it.
entries.pitfalls: Used to dismiss your own justified inferences ('maybe I'm just on the ladder') can be a form of gaslighting yourself out of valid pattern-recognition. Also, in adversarial settings (negotiation, court), inferring from behavior is necessary and correct. The model is most useful in trust-relevant relationships, not all situations.
entries.origin: Chris Argyris, Harvard Business School organizational psychologist, 1970s; developed in his work on 'theories of action' and popularized in Peter Senge's 'The Fifth Discipline' (1990) and Argyris's 'Overcoming Organizational Defenses' (1990).

entries.name: Lindy Effect
entries.oneLiner: For non-perishable things — ideas, books, technologies — every additional year of survival roughly doubles their expected remaining life.
entries.description: Originating in observations about Broadway shows and formalized by Mandelbrot and Taleb, the Lindy effect says the future life expectancy of a non-perishable item is proportional to its current age. A book in print for 50 years is likely to be read 50 more; a 2-year-old fad is likely to vanish in 2. It's a heuristic for filtering signal from hype: time is an unforgiving editor, and survival is information. Crucially it applies only to non-perishables — the opposite is true for humans, machines, and perishable goods, where each year reduces expected remaining life.
entries.example: Stoicism (~2,300 years old) is likely to outlive the latest productivity-influencer framework. Euclid's Elements has been taught for 2,300 years; expect another century at least. A JavaScript framework released 18 months ago is more likely to be deprecated than to define the next decade.
entries.howToApply: When choosing what to read, eat, build with, or believe, weight options by their age. Default to long-surviving books (>30 years) over this year's bestseller. For technology choices in a long-lived system, prefer the boring, decades-old option (Postgres, email, plain text) unless you have a specific reason. Inverse: assume new fashions, new diets, and new economic theories will not survive the decade.
entries.pitfalls: Lindy is a base rate, not a law — old ideas can be wrong (bloodletting lasted millennia), and genuine paradigm shifts do occur. It also doesn't apply to perishables or technologies in active obsolescence. And 'old' must mean continuously surviving in real use, not merely catalogued.
entries.origin: Albert Goldman in The New Republic, 1964; named the 'Lindy Law' by Mandelbrot, 1982; sharpened by Taleb in Antifragile, 2012.

entries.name: Murphy's Law
entries.oneLiner: Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong — so design for failure, not for hope.
entries.description: Murphy's Law is widely attributed to Edward A. Murphy Jr., an aerospace engineer working on the U.S. Air Force's MX981 rocket-sled experiments at Edwards Air Force Base in 1949. After a technician wired strain-gauge sensors backward (every one of them), Murphy reportedly remarked that if there were a way to do it wrong, someone would. Project director George Nichols formalized the phrase, and Major John Paul Stapp publicized it. Beyond folklore, the law encodes a serious engineering discipline: in any sufficiently complex system with many interacting parts, low-probability failures will eventually occur because there are so many opportunities for them. It's the intuition behind defensive programming, redundancy, fail-safes, fault trees, and chaos engineering. The law isn't fatalism — it's a call to make failure modes explicit and tolerable.
entries.example: AWS's 2017 S3 outage in us-east-1 stemmed from a single mistyped command in a maintenance script that took down a far larger swath of capacity than intended; the playbook had no guard for that input. The Therac-25 radiation overdoses (1985-87) happened because race conditions that 'couldn't' occur did, repeatedly. Netflix's Chaos Monkey deliberately kills production instances precisely because Murphy's Law is real — better to discover the failure on a Tuesday afternoon than at 3 a.m.
entries.howToApply: In engineering: enumerate failure modes (FMEA), assume every external dependency will be unavailable at the worst time, add timeouts and circuit breakers, run game-days. In planning: ask 'what's the dumbest thing that could break this?' and budget time for it (typically add 30-50% to estimates). In life: keep backups, carry a spare key, leave early for the airport, have a Plan B for important conversations. Pre-mortems (Klein) are Murphy's Law operationalized — imagine the project failed and write down why.
entries.pitfalls: Used carelessly, it justifies endless paranoia, gold-plating, and analysis paralysis — you can't defend against every possibility, and trying to bankrupts the project. The law is about probability over time, not certainty in any single instance; treating it as inevitable doom leads to learned helplessness. Also avoid using it to excuse incompetence ('Murphy got us') when the real cause was negligence or skipped reviews.
entries.origin: Originated in the U.S. Air Force MX981 rocket-sled tests (1949), credited to Edward A. Murphy Jr. and popularized by Major John Paul Stapp. Documented in Nick T. Spark, 'A History of Murphy's Law' (2006). For the engineering discipline, see Charles Perrow, 'Normal Accidents' (1984), and Nancy Leveson, 'Engineering a Safer World' (2011).

entries.name: Occam's Razor
entries.oneLiner: Among competing explanations that fit the evidence equally, prefer the one with the fewest assumptions.
entries.description: Occam's Razor is a principle of theory selection: do not multiply entities beyond necessity. It's not a law of nature — simpler explanations aren't guaranteed correct — but a tie-breaker that favors falsifiable, parsimonious hypotheses over baroque ones. It functions as a prior, not a verdict.
entries.example: Your laptop is slow today. Hypothesis A: a Chrome tab is hogging RAM. Hypothesis B: a state-actor APT has compromised your firmware. Both 'explain' the symptom; A requires fewer new entities, so you check Activity Monitor first.
entries.howToApply: When weighing two explanations: (1) Count the new entities each requires (hidden actors, conspiracies, novel mechanisms). (2) Pick the one with fewer to investigate first. (3) Only escalate to the complex explanation when the simple one is empirically ruled out, not when it merely feels boring.
entries.pitfalls: It's regularly misquoted as 'the simplest answer is right' — it isn't. Reality is sometimes complex (immune system, financial markets, quantum mechanics). The razor breaks when models have different fits to evidence; it only adjudicates among models with equal predictive power. And what counts as 'simple' is theory-laden.
entries.origin: William of Ockham, 14th-century English Franciscan friar, though the principle predates him in Aristotle and Ptolemy. The classical Latin formulation 'entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem' was actually coined by John Punch in 1639.

entries.name: Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)
entries.oneLiner: Roughly 80% of outcomes come from 20% of inputs, so identify and double down on the vital few.
entries.description: An empirical heuristic noting that outputs are rarely distributed evenly across inputs. A small fraction of customers, code, or effort tends to drive the majority of revenue, bugs, or results. It is a power-law observation, not a precise law — the split could be 90/10 or 70/30, but the asymmetry is the point. Use it to find leverage rather than to grind on every task equally.
entries.example: A SaaS founder reviews her revenue and finds 3 of 50 customers generate 78% of monthly recurring revenue. She reallocates her support team to provide white-glove service to those three accounts and stops spending evening hours on long-tail trial users.
entries.howToApply: Once a quarter, list your tasks/clients/projects and rank them by output (revenue, learning, impact). Cross out the bottom half and ask: what would change if I stopped doing these? Then schedule one calendar block per week dedicated only to expanding the top 20%.
entries.pitfalls: The numbers are not literal — chasing an exact 80/20 split is misuse. Some domains (safety, security, parenting) require attention to the long tail; you cannot 80/20 a building inspection. It also tempts neglect of foundational work that compounds slowly.
entries.origin: Vilfredo Pareto observed Italian land-ownership distribution in 1906; Joseph M. Juran reframed it as the 'vital few and trivial many' management principle in 1941.

entries.name: Systems Thinking
entries.oneLiner: See the world as interconnected stocks, flows, and feedback loops instead of isolated cause-and-effect events.
entries.description: Systems thinking, developed by Jay Forrester at MIT and popularized by Donella Meadows, models behavior as the product of structure: stocks (accumulations), flows (rates), and feedback loops (reinforcing or balancing). It explains why well-intentioned interventions backfire (policy resistance), why problems recur after being 'solved,' and where high-leverage interventions actually live. Meadows' essay 'Leverage Points' ranks intervention types from low (parameters, taxes) to high (paradigms, the goal of the system itself).
entries.example: Adding lanes to a highway often increases congestion within years (induced demand): the reinforcing loop between road capacity and driving behavior swamps the parameter change. Or: cutting customer-support headcount lowers cost short-term but raises churn, which lowers revenue, which triggers more cuts.
entries.howToApply: When facing a recurring problem, sketch a causal-loop diagram: identify the stock you care about, the inflows and outflows, and the feedback loops controlling each. Ask 'where is the delay?' (delays cause overshoot) and 'what is the goal of this system, and is it the goal we want?' Prefer interventions at the goal/paradigm level over parameter tweaks.
entries.pitfalls: Diagrams can become baroque art projects with no decision attached. Also, complex systems are partly unknowable — overconfident system maps are just bigger maps with the same Korzybski problem. Use systems thinking to generate hypotheses, not certainties.
entries.origin: Jay Forrester (Industrial Dynamics, 1961); Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems, posthumous 2008.

entries.name: The Cathedral Effect — Ceiling Height Shapes Cognition
entries.oneLiner: High ceilings prime abstract, expansive thinking; low ceilings prime concrete, detail-oriented thinking — the room shapes the mind.
entries.description: Meyers-Levy and Zhu's 2007 Journal of Consumer Research paper 'The Influence of Ceiling Height: The Effect of Priming on the Type of Processing People Use' showed experimentally that 10-foot ceilings activated concepts of freedom and abstraction, producing more creative, relational, and big-picture thinking, while 8-foot ceilings activated confinement and detail orientation, producing more focused, concrete, item-specific processing. The mechanism is conceptual priming: cathedrals were built tall not by accident but to evoke transcendence; cubicles are short not by accident but to focus you on the spreadsheet. Subsequent work in embodied cognition (Lakoff & Johnson; Williams & Bargh) extends the finding — physical warmth primes interpersonal warmth, weight primes importance, distance primes abstraction. The practical upshot: creative work and detail work want different rooms.
entries.example: A product team is stuck in a windowless 8-foot-ceiling conference room debating whether to pivot. Three hours of detail-grinding produces no decision. They walk to the lobby — 20-foot ceiling, glass walls — and within 40 minutes have reframed the question entirely and chosen a direction. The next day they return to the small room to make the implementation plan, where focused detail work is exactly what's needed.
entries.howToApply: Match the space to the task. For strategy, vision, brainstorming, and reframing, seek out high-ceilinged or open spaces — atriums, libraries, parks, walks. For execution, debugging, line-edits, and detailed analysis, use enclosed, smaller-scale spaces. If you can't change rooms, change cues: open windows for abstract work, close blinds for detail work; stand for ideation, sit for editing. When designing offices, reserve at least one tall, open space for non-routine thinking and don't fill it with desks.
entries.pitfalls: Effect sizes in the original studies are modest (Cohen's d roughly 0.3–0.5) and the broader embodied-cognition literature has had notable replication failures (e.g., Bargh's elderly-priming, weight-importance studies). Treat the effect as a nudge, not a determinant — don't blame a bad strategy on a low ceiling. Also, individual differences swamp the effect for many people, especially those who do their best thinking in cramped, familiar spaces.
entries.origin: Joan Meyers-Levy & Rui (Juliet) Zhu, 'The Influence of Ceiling Height: The Effect of Priming on the Type of Processing People Use,' Journal of Consumer Research, Vol. 34, No. 2 (August 2007), pp. 174–186. Broader context: George Lakoff & Mark Johnson, 'Metaphors We Live By' (1980); embodied cognition program in cognitive science.

entries.name: Via Negativa — Improvement by Subtraction
entries.oneLiner: You often improve a system faster by removing what's harmful than by adding what seems helpful.
entries.description: Borrowed from apophatic theology (defining God by what God is not), via negativa was popularized by Nassim Nicholas Taleb in 'Antifragile' as an epistemic and practical heuristic: we know with greater certainty what is bad than what is good, so subtractive interventions are more robust than additive ones. Removing a known harm has predictable upside and limited side-effects; adding a new intervention multiplies unknown unknowns. The Stoics applied the same logic ethically — 'the chief task in life is simply this: to identify and separate matters so that I can say to myself which are externals not under my control' (Epictetus) — by stripping away false beliefs, attachments, and desires rather than acquiring virtues.
entries.example: A team's deploys keep breaking. The instinct is to add more tests, more reviewers, more dashboards. Via negativa says: first remove the three flaky test suites everyone ignores, delete the two unused services, and stop the Friday afternoon deploy window. Failure rate drops 60% before any new tooling is built.
entries.howToApply: Before adding a new habit, tool, person, meeting, or rule, ask 'What can I remove that would produce the same or better effect?' Keep a 'stop-doing' list alongside your to-do list. In health, fix sleep and remove processed foods before adding supplements. In code, delete dead paths before refactoring. In writing, cut 20% before polishing.
entries.pitfalls: Can be weaponized to justify gutting useful complexity ('Chesterton's Fence' violations) or to avoid the harder work of building. Subtraction has limits — at some point you actually need to add the new feature, the new hire, the new habit. Also, removal is socially costlier than addition because losses are visible and gains are diffuse.
entries.origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 'Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder' (Random House, 2012), ch. 'Via Negativa.' Roots in apophatic / negative theology (Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides) and Stoic askesis (Epictetus, 'Discourses' II.5).

entries.name: Anchoring
entries.oneLiner: The first number you see warps every subsequent estimate, even when it's obviously irrelevant.
entries.description: Anchoring is the tendency for an initial reference point to bias subsequent numerical judgments. In Tversky & Kahneman's original demonstration, a spun wheel of fortune showing 10 or 65 shifted participants' estimates of the percentage of African nations in the UN, even though everyone knew the wheel was random. Anchoring is one of the most replicable effects in behavioral economics.
entries.example: A house listed at $1.2M frames a $1.05M offer as a 'discount,' even if comparables suggest $950K is fair. A menu's $95 steak makes the $48 pasta seem reasonable. In salary negotiation, whoever names the first number typically captures more of the surplus.
entries.howToApply: Decide your reservation price and target before hearing the other side's number. When given an anchor, write down an independent estimate from first principles before responding. In negotiations, anchor first when you have good information; defer when you don't. For purchases, research comparable prices before exposure to the seller's number.
entries.pitfalls: Some 'anchoring' studies in priming research have failed to replicate, but the core numerical-anchoring effect is robust. Don't anchor aggressively when you're under-informed; an extreme anchor can blow up the deal or signal bad faith.
entries.origin: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1974, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases,' Science 185:1124-1131.

entries.name: Availability Heuristic
entries.oneLiner: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual frequency.
entries.description: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where probability is estimated by ease of recall. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events feel more probable than they are. It explains why people overestimate plane-crash and shark-attack risk, and underestimate cardiovascular disease (which kills ~1 in 4 Americans but rarely makes the front page).
entries.example: After watching a news cycle on a kidnapping, parents drive their kids to school, exposing them to a much higher per-mile fatality risk than the abduction they're avoiding. After a friend's startup IPO, you overestimate the probability that yours will too.
entries.howToApply: For any risk decision, look up base rates before reacting. Ask: 'Am I scared because the data says so, or because the example is vivid?' Maintain a 'boring statistics' bookmark folder (CDC, actuarial tables, BLS) for common decisions. Wait 24-48 hours before acting on news-driven emotional impulses.
entries.pitfalls: Availability sometimes tracks reality (frequent things really are more recallable). The bias is in the asymmetric weighting of vividness vs. frequency, not in memory-based reasoning per se.
entries.origin: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1973, 'Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability,' Cognitive Psychology 5:207-232.

entries.name: Confirmation Bias
entries.oneLiner: We seek, remember, and weight evidence that confirms what we already believe, and discount what doesn't.
entries.description: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that supports prior beliefs. It is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology and operates across politics, hiring, medical diagnosis, and investing. Critically, it is mostly unconscious; even experts who know about it still exhibit it.
entries.example: An investor convinced a stock will rise reads bullish analyst notes, dismisses the bearish quarterly report as 'noise,' and ends up holding through a 40% drawdown. A hiring manager who 'liked' a candidate in the first 30 seconds spends the rest of the interview asking questions whose answers fit that first impression.
entries.howToApply: Before a decision, write down what evidence would change your mind, then deliberately search for it. Steel-man the opposing view in writing. Use a pre-mortem: 'It's one year later and this decision failed. Why?' For high-stakes calls, assign a teammate the role of 'red-teamer' whose job is to argue the other side.
entries.pitfalls: Don't confuse it with simply having strong evidence; Bayesian updating still favors well-supported priors. Also: 'debiasing' training has weak transfer effects in the lab; structural fixes (checklists, blind review, pre-registration) outperform willpower.
entries.origin: Peter Wason, 1960 (2-4-6 rule-discovery task); concept popularized by Raymond Nickerson's 1998 review in Review of General Psychology.

entries.name: Default Effect
entries.oneLiner: People disproportionately stick with whatever option is preselected, so defaults often determine outcomes more than preferences do.
entries.description: In the absence of strong preferences, the default option carries enormous weight because changing it requires effort, attention, and a tolerance for regret. Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein's classic 2003 Science paper showed organ donation rates of ~12% in opt-in countries (Germany, UK) versus ~99% in otherwise similar opt-out countries (Austria, France) — driven almost entirely by the default. Similar effects appear in 401(k) enrollment, insurance plans, and software settings.
entries.example: When companies switched from opt-in to automatic 401(k) enrollment after the Pension Protection Act of 2006, participation among new hires jumped from roughly 50–60% to 90%+, even though the contribution decision was nominally identical.
entries.howToApply: 1) Audit your own defaults: phone home screen, browser homepage, recurring grocery order, contribution rates. 2) Set defaults toward your future self's interests (auto-transfer to savings, default to water not soda by what you stock). 3) When designing for others (a team, a product), choose defaults deliberately — they are not neutral.
entries.pitfalls: Defaults can be manipulative when they exploit inattention rather than serve people (dark patterns: pre-checked add-ons, auto-renewing subscriptions). For high-stakes, well-considered choices (mortgages, medical decisions), defaults matter less because people actually deliberate.
entries.origin: Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein, 'Do Defaults Save Lives?' (Science, 2003); popularized in Thaler and Sunstein's Nudge (2008).

entries.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
entries.oneLiner: People with little skill in a domain often overestimate their ability because the skills needed to do well also let you judge your performance.
entries.description: In Kruger and Dunning's original 1999 study, students in the bottom quartile on grammar, logic, and humor tests rated themselves around the 60th percentile. The same metacognitive deficit that produces poor performance also blocks accurate self-assessment. Interestingly, top performers tended to slightly underestimate themselves, assuming tasks easy for them were easy for others.
entries.example: A new manager who has run two meetings rates themselves as 'above average' at facilitation, while a 20-year veteran who has run thousands rates themselves a 7/10 because they vividly remember their failures.
entries.howToApply: 1) On any new skill, assume you're worse than you feel for the first ~50 hours. 2) Seek objective benchmarks: tests, peer ratings, recorded performance, paying clients. 3) Ask 'what would an expert in this find wrong with my work?'. 4) Track confidence vs. outcome over time to calibrate. 5) Default to humility on unfamiliar topics, especially when you feel strongly.
entries.pitfalls: Frequently misinterpreted as 'dumb people don't know they're dumb'; the original effect is about domain-specific incompetence, not general intelligence. Some statisticians (Nuhfer et al., 2017; McIntosh et al., 2019) argue much of the pattern reflects regression to the mean and noise, not a real metacognitive bias. Treat the size of the effect with skepticism even if the direction is real.
entries.origin: Justin Kruger & David Dunning, 'Unskilled and Unaware of It' (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1999).

entries.name: Endowment Effect
entries.oneLiner: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire it.
entries.description: Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler's 1990 mug experiments showed that subjects randomly given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice the price to sell it as buyers would pay, despite identical objective value. The effect is grounded in loss aversion: losses loom about twice as large as equivalent gains.
entries.example: Homeowners price their homes above market and refuse offers near appraisal. Employees turn down better job offers because changing means giving up familiar perks. Investors hold losing stocks too long because selling 'realizes' the loss.
entries.howToApply: Run the 'reversal test': if you didn't already own this stock, house, job, or relationship, would you buy in at today's price and terms? If no, that is your answer. For negotiations, frame concessions as gains for the counterparty rather than losses.
entries.pitfalls: Recent work (Plott & Zeiler 2005, 2007) shows much of the effect disappears with proper experimental procedures and experienced traders, suggesting some 'endowment' is misunderstanding of the task. The effect is real but weaker for fungible goods (cash, commodities) and for traders with market experience.
entries.origin: Term coined by Richard Thaler in 1980; canonical demonstration by Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler in Journal of Political Economy, 1990.

entries.name: Halo Effect
entries.oneLiner: One positive trait, especially attractiveness, contaminates judgment of unrelated traits like intelligence or honesty.
entries.description: The halo effect is a cognitive bias where overall impression of a person, brand, or thing colors evaluation of specific attributes. Edward Thorndike named it in 1920 after observing officers rated soldiers high on every trait once they liked them overall. It also runs in reverse (the 'horns effect').
entries.example: Attractive defendants receive lighter sentences in mock-jury studies (Stewart, 1980). Apple's iPod halo lifted Mac sales in the mid-2000s. In hiring, a candidate from a prestigious school is rated higher on coding ability before any code is seen.
entries.howToApply: Decouple judgments: when evaluating a hire, score each dimension independently before seeing the overall package, ideally blind. Use structured interviews and rubrics. When you catch yourself liking someone instantly, ask 'what specifically have they shown me about competence X?'
entries.pitfalls: Hard to debias by willpower alone, since it operates pre-consciously. 'Just be aware of it' has weak evidence; structural fixes (blind review, separated ratings) work better. Also confused with simple correlation: attractive people may genuinely have advantages from a lifetime of better treatment.
entries.origin: Edward Thorndike, 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings,' Journal of Applied Psychology (1920).

entries.name: Hindsight Bias
entries.oneLiner: After an event, we remember having 'known it all along,' which corrupts how we learn from outcomes.
entries.description: Hindsight bias is the tendency, once an outcome is known, to overestimate how predictable it was beforehand. Fischhoff's classic studies showed people who learned an event's outcome reported they would have predicted it; people without the outcome rarely did. It distorts post-mortems, lawsuit verdicts, and personal regret.
entries.example: After a startup's IPO, founders' early bets seem 'obviously brilliant'; after its collapse, the same bets seem 'obviously stupid.' After 2008, every financial commentator 'saw the housing crash coming,' though contemporaneous predictions were mixed. Juries judging a doctor's pre-incident decisions know the bad outcome and rate the decision as more negligent.
entries.howToApply: Write down predictions with timestamps before outcomes are known (a 'forecasting journal' or tools like Manifold). In post-mortems, separate decision quality from outcome quality, judging the decision against what was knowable at the time. When evaluating others' past calls, ask: 'What did the consensus say then?'
entries.pitfalls: Don't overcorrect into 'no one could have known': sometimes warning signs really were available and ignored. The fix is documented foresight, not blanket forgiveness.
entries.origin: Baruch Fischhoff, 1975, 'Hindsight ≠ Foresight: The effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty,' Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 1:288-299.

entries.name: IKEA Effect
entries.oneLiner: People overvalue things they partially built themselves, regardless of objective quality.
entries.description: Norton, Mochon, and Ariely (2012) showed subjects who assembled IKEA boxes, folded origami, or built Lego sets bid significantly more for their own creations than equivalent items made by others, and rated their amateur work close to expert work. The effect requires successful completion and genuine effort, not just any labor.
entries.example: Founders routinely overvalue their own startups and resist pivots. Home cooks rate their own meals higher than diners do. Crypto holders defend tokens whose whitepapers they read carefully even after fundamentals deteriorate.
entries.howToApply: Before big decisions about something you built, get a third party with no skin in the game to price it or critique it. When selling something you made, anchor on comparable market sales, not on hours spent. Conversely, exploit it ethically: customers who help configure your product retain better.
entries.pitfalls: Overlaps with sunk-cost fallacy and endowment effect; do not let pride in construction lock you into a losing project. The effect collapses if the build fails, so half-built projects can flip to aversion.
entries.origin: Michael I. Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely, Journal of Consumer Psychology, 2012.

entries.name: In-Group Bias (Minimal Group Paradigm)
entries.oneLiner: Even arbitrary group labels make people favor their own side and discriminate against outsiders.
entries.description: Henri Tajfel's minimal group experiments (1971) showed subjects assigned to meaningless groups (e.g., 'preferred Klee over Kandinsky') still allocated more resources to in-group members and were willing to give up absolute gains to maximize relative advantage. This grew into Social Identity Theory.
entries.example: Sports rivalries, political tribalism, the 'Robbers Cave' experiment (Sherif, 1954). In organizations, team-vs-team budget fights often run hotter than the underlying stakes warrant. Online, arbitrary fandom labels predict harsh treatment of out-group strangers.
entries.howToApply: Notice when 'us vs them' framing kicks in — especially when the group is freshly invented (a new team name, a new product brand). Build superordinate goals that require cross-group cooperation; this reduces bias more reliably than diversity training alone. Personally, name your tribes and ask whether the threat is real.
entries.pitfalls: Some classic studies (Robbers Cave, Stanford Prison) had serious methodological and ethical problems and were partly stage-managed; do not over-cite them. Implicit bias trainings show small, often zero, behavior change in meta-analyses (Forscher et al., 2019), so beware quick fixes.
entries.origin: Henri Tajfel and colleagues, 'Social categorization and intergroup behaviour,' European Journal of Social Psychology (1971).

entries.name: Loss Aversion in Investing
entries.oneLiner: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good, causing investors to sell winners early and ride losers down.
entries.description: Kahneman & Tversky's Prospect Theory (1979) found that people weigh losses about 2x as heavily as equivalent gains. In investing this manifests as the 'disposition effect' (Shefrin & Statman, 1985): selling winners to lock in gains while holding losers to avoid realizing the loss — exactly the opposite of optimal tax-loss harvesting. It also drives panic selling at market bottoms and excessive caution at market tops. Bogle wrote that investors' biggest enemy is 'the man in the mirror.'
entries.example: March 2020: an investor watches her index fund fall 30% in a month and sells to 'stop the bleeding.' She waits to re-enter 'when it's safe' and misses most of the rebound. Behaviorally identical investors who simply did nothing finished 2020 up double digits.
entries.howToApply: Automate contributions so emotions don't gate investing. Look at your portfolio quarterly at most — daily checking amplifies loss aversion (Benartzi & Thaler's 'myopic loss aversion,' 1995). Pre-commit a written Investment Policy Statement specifying your asset allocation and rebalancing rule; follow it mechanically in drawdowns. For tax purposes, harvest losses systematically rather than emotionally.
entries.pitfalls: Loss aversion has faced real replication scrutiny — Gal & Rucker (2018) and others argue the 2:1 ratio is context-dependent and sometimes vanishes for low-stakes or non-monetary decisions. Don't over-apply: sometimes selling a position genuinely is correct because the thesis broke. The bias is about reflexive emotional asymmetry, not all sell decisions.
entries.origin: Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk,' Econometrica (1979) — work for which Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics.

entries.name: Mere Exposure Effect
entries.oneLiner: Repeated exposure to something, even subliminal, tends to increase liking for it without any other reason.
entries.description: Robert Zajonc demonstrated in 1968 that simply seeing a stimulus more often (nonsense words, Chinese characters, faces) made people rate it more positively. The effect operates without conscious recognition and is one of the most robustly replicated findings in social psychology, with a meta-analytic effect size around r = 0.26 (Bornstein, 1989).
entries.example: You like a song more after the third radio play. Logos that seemed ugly become acceptable after a rebrand period. Classmates who sit nearer to you become friends more often than equally compatible classmates across the room (Festinger, Schachter, Back, 1950).
entries.howToApply: To build a relationship, increase low-pressure incidental contact (shared lunches, recurring meetings) before pitching anything. For products, prioritize sustained low-key visibility over one big launch. Personally, audit which preferences are real and which are 'I just keep seeing this.'
entries.pitfalls: Overexposure causes satiation and reversal. Negative initial reaction can be amplified, not softened, by repetition (e.g., divisive ads). The effect is weaker when the stimulus is consciously evaluated than when it is briefly or subliminally shown.
entries.origin: Robert Zajonc, 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1968).

entries.name: Negativity Bias
entries.oneLiner: Bad is stronger than good: negative events grab more attention, weight, and memory than equivalent positives.
entries.description: Negativity bias is the asymmetric weighting of negative information across attention, learning, memory, and decisions. Baumeister et al.'s 'Bad is Stronger than Good' (2001) and Rozin & Royzman's 'Negativity Bias, Negativity Dominance, and Contagion' (2001) document this across domains: one criticism outweighs five compliments, one bad meal taints a restaurant's reputation, lost money hurts more than equal gains.
entries.example: A glowing performance review with one critical line: you ruminate on the criticism for a week. One bad Yelp review sinks a small restaurant despite 50 good ones. News feeds optimize for outrage because negative headlines drive more clicks per impression.
entries.howToApply: Use a 5:1 'positivity ratio' rule of thumb in feedback to others (Gottman's marriage research finds healthy couples run roughly 5:1 positive to negative interactions). Keep a daily 'three good things' log; meta-analyses (Bolier et al. 2013) find modest but real well-being effects. Audit your information diet: remove sources whose business model is anger.
entries.pitfalls: Don't suppress legitimate negative signals; pain and fear exist for good reasons. The Losada/Fredrickson '2.9013 ratio' was retracted as mathematically invalid (Brown, Sokal & Friedman 2013), and broad 'positive psychology' claims have a mixed replication record.
entries.origin: Roy Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer, & Kathleen Vohs, 2001, 'Bad is Stronger than Good,' Review of General Psychology 5:323-370; concurrently Paul Rozin & Edward Royzman, 2001.

entries.name: Recency Bias
entries.oneLiner: We overweight what happened recently and assume it will continue, ignoring longer-run base rates.
entries.description: Recency bias is the tendency to give disproportionate weight to recent events when forecasting or judging. It's related to the availability heuristic but specifically about temporal proximity. In memory research, it shows up as the 'recency effect' in serial recall (Murdock 1962); in forecasting, it manifests as extrapolating recent trends.
entries.example: After a strong year, retail investors pour money into the previous year's top-performing fund category, which historically reverts (DALBAR's annual studies estimate this 'behavior gap' at ~1-2% per year of underperformance). Managers rate employees mostly on the last month before review. After one bad date, you conclude you 'always pick wrong.'
entries.howToApply: For any forecast, look at 10+ years of history, not 1-2. Use rolling averages and base rates instead of point-in-time snapshots. For performance reviews, keep a running notes file for each report so the last two weeks don't dominate. In investing, set an asset allocation and rebalance on a calendar, not on news.
entries.pitfalls: Recent data sometimes really does carry the most signal (regime changes, structural breaks). The skill is asking whether the underlying generator has actually changed; if not, mean reversion usually wins.
entries.origin: Memory effect documented by Bennet Murdock, 1962, 'The serial position effect of free recall,' Journal of Experimental Psychology 64:482-488; decision-making applications throughout the heuristics-and-biases tradition (Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky 1982).

entries.name: Spotlight Effect
entries.oneLiner: We dramatically overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, mistakes, and quirks.
entries.description: Gilovich, Medvec, and Savitsky (2000) had Cornell students wear an embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room of peers; wearers estimated about 50% would notice, but only ~25% actually did, and even fewer remembered later. The bias stems from egocentric anchoring: we cannot easily simulate others' attention, which is mostly on themselves.
entries.example: Stumbling over a word in a presentation feels devastating; almost no one in the audience remembers it the next day. A bad haircut feels universally noticed; coworkers usually don't comment because they barely registered it.
entries.howToApply: Before social anxiety derails action, ask: 'Will anyone here remember this in 48 hours?' If no, proceed. Use this to lower the cost of asking dumb questions, public speaking, dating, networking, and looking foolish while learning a new skill.
entries.pitfalls: Do not over-apply this in genuinely high-stakes professional or reputational contexts where people are evaluating you on purpose (interviews, performance reviews, public-facing roles). The effect is about incidental observation, not deliberate evaluation.
entries.origin: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec, and Kenneth Savitsky, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000.

entries.name: Streetlight Effect
entries.oneLiner: We search for answers where it's easy to look, not where the truth is — like the drunk searching for his keys under the streetlight because that's where the light is.
entries.description: The Streetlight Effect (or 'drunkard's search') is a methodological bias in which investigators choose what to study based on availability of data or ease of measurement, rather than relevance to the question. The parable, traceable at least to Nasreddin Hodja's tales and popularized in modern form by Abraham Kaplan in 'The Conduct of Inquiry' (1964), captures something pervasive: we measure what's measurable, and then mistake the measurable for the important. It's an observational-selection bias that systematically distorts science, business analytics, journalism, and self-knowledge. The effect compounds with confirmation bias: once you've looked under the streetlight long enough, you start finding patterns there and assume that's where the answer must be.
entries.example: Drug discovery historically focused on targets that were 'druggable' (easy to bind small molecules to) rather than targets most relevant to disease — leaving roughly 80% of disease-relevant proteins unaddressed for decades. Productivity research over-relies on knowledge-worker self-reports because they're easy to collect, while the harder-to-measure questions (deep work quality, creative output) get less attention. In personal finance, people obsess over coffee spending (visible, measurable) while ignoring lifestyle creep on rent and cars (larger but less salient). Election forecasters in 2016 leaned on polling data because it existed, even where it was known to be poor for the question being asked.
entries.howToApply: Before starting an investigation, ask: 'what's the question I actually care about, and would the data I'm about to collect answer it — or am I picking it because it's available?' If it's the latter, name the gap explicitly and either commission better data, use proxies with known biases, or change the question to one your data can honestly address. In product analytics, distinguish 'metrics that are easy to log' from 'metrics that capture user value.' In introspection, journal the things you avoid noticing, not just the ones you track.
entries.pitfalls: The bias is not avoidable in absolute terms — every investigation has data constraints, and some streetlight searching is rational when the cost of better data exceeds its expected value. The error is not searching under the light, but forgetting that you did, and over-claiming. Also, the joke version assumes the keys aren't under the light; sometimes the easy-to-measure thing genuinely is the answer. The real skill is calibrating how much to update based on streetlight evidence.
entries.origin: The parable appears in Nasreddin/Hodja folk tales and was given its modern methodological framing by Abraham Kaplan, 'The Conduct of Inquiry: Methodology for Behavioral Science' (1964), pp. 11. See also David H. Freedman, 'Why Scientific Studies Are So Often Wrong: The Streetlight Effect,' Discover Magazine (2010).

entries.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
entries.oneLiner: We keep investing in losing courses because of what we've already spent, even though that money is gone either way.
entries.description: The sunk cost fallacy is continued commitment to an endeavor based on previously invested (and unrecoverable) resources, rather than expected future value. Rational decision theory says only marginal future costs and benefits should matter; humans systematically violate this. Concorde's continued funding despite known unprofitability is the textbook case ('Concorde fallacy').
entries.example: Sitting through a bad 3-hour movie because you already paid; staying in a 4-year relationship because you've 'invested 4 years'; finishing a graduate program you hate because you're 'already halfway through.' Companies pour another $50M into a doomed product because they've spent $200M.
entries.howToApply: Reframe every ongoing decision as: 'If I were starting fresh today with no history, would I begin this?' If no, exit. Set kill-criteria before starting projects ('I'll abandon this if X by month 6'). Separate the accountant's view (sunk costs are zero) from the storyteller's view (which protects ego).
entries.pitfalls: Sometimes 'persistence pays off' really is correct: if completing the project unlocks a step-function payoff (vesting, credentials, network effects), the marginal calculus may favor finishing. The fallacy is treating past spend itself as a reason; legitimate reasons are always forward-looking.
entries.origin: Concept formalized by Hal Arkes & Catherine Blumer, 1985, 'The Psychology of Sunk Cost,' Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35:124-140.

entries.name: Survivorship Bias
entries.oneLiner: We study the winners and ignore the graveyard, drawing lessons from a sample that excludes failures.
entries.description: Survivorship bias occurs when analysis focuses only on entities that 'survived' some selection process, ignoring those that didn't, leading to overly optimistic conclusions. The classic illustration is Abraham Wald's WWII work on bomber armor: the planes that returned showed bullet holes in the wings and tail, but the Statistical Research Group correctly inferred the engines and cockpit needed armor because planes hit there didn't make it back.
entries.example: Reading 'how I built a $10M startup' Twitter threads as a playbook ignores the thousands of founders who followed identical advice and went bankrupt. Mutual fund rankings that only show currently-existing funds inflate average returns by 1-2% per year because closed/merged underperformers are deleted.
entries.howToApply: Before copying a strategy, ask: 'What's the base rate of failure for people who tried this?' Seek out failed cases explicitly (post-mortems, bankruptcy filings, abandoned-project blogs). When evaluating performance data, demand survivor-free databases (e.g., CRSP for stocks).
entries.pitfalls: Survivors sometimes really do have signal worth learning from, especially when the survival mechanism is skill rather than luck. The fix isn't to ignore winners but to also study comparable losers.
entries.origin: Statistical concept; named explicitly in finance/management literature in the 1990s. Wald's bomber analysis (Statistical Research Group, Columbia, 1943) is the canonical example.

entries.name: The Map Is Not the Territory
entries.oneLiner: Every model, metric, or mental picture is a simplification — never confuse the description of reality with reality itself.
entries.description: Coined by Alfred Korzybski in general semantics, this principle warns that representations (maps, financial models, diagnoses, stereotypes) necessarily omit detail. A useful map is wrong in known, bounded ways; danger arises when we forget the omissions and treat the model as the thing. The corollary: when map and terrain disagree, trust the terrain.
entries.example: GPS routing drivers off a closed bridge into a lake — the map said 'road,' the territory said 'water.' Or: a 2008 risk model rating mortgage tranches AAA because historical default correlations were mapped from a non-crisis territory.
entries.howToApply: Before acting on a model, write down (a) what it deliberately ignores and (b) the conditions under which it breaks. Schedule periodic 'ground truth' checks: talk to a customer instead of reading the dashboard, walk the factory floor, read the actual contract. When a metric and a person's lived experience disagree, investigate before dismissing either.
entries.pitfalls: Used as an excuse to dismiss any quantitative model ('numbers can't capture reality'). Models are still indispensable — the move is calibrated humility, not nihilism. Also, the territory you observe is itself filtered through perceptual maps.
entries.origin: Alfred Korzybski, Science and Sanity, 1933.

entries.name: Zeigarnik Effect
entries.oneLiner: Unfinished tasks occupy mental bandwidth more than completed ones, intruding on attention until closed.
entries.description: Bluma Zeigarnik's 1927 dissertation found waiters could recall unpaid orders better than paid ones, and lab subjects remembered interrupted tasks roughly twice as well as completed tasks. Later replications (notably Masicampo & Baumeister 2011) show that simply making a concrete plan to finish a task can release the cognitive grip even before completion.
entries.example: Cliffhanger episode endings on Netflix drive auto-play because the unresolved plot keeps your attention engaged. Open browser tabs you 'will read later' silently consume working memory until you either read, save, or close them.
entries.howToApply: When a task intrudes at night, write down a specific next step and time ('Tuesday 9am: email Sam draft v2'); studies show this defuses rumination as effectively as finishing it. Close loops daily: declare end-of-day, capture open items in one trusted list, then disengage.
entries.pitfalls: Replication of Zeigarnik's original recall ratio has been mixed; the strong 2:1 effect is unreliable, but the rumination-from-open-loops mechanism holds up well. Do not use it as an excuse to leave everything half-done as a 'motivation hack'.
entries.origin: Bluma Zeigarnik, working under Kurt Lewin in Berlin, 1927 dissertation.

entries.name: 10-10-10 Rule
entries.oneLiner: Ask how you'll feel about this decision in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years to neutralize emotional distortion.
entries.description: Welch's heuristic forces you to evaluate a decision across three time horizons simultaneously. The 10-minute horizon honors immediate emotion; 10 months captures medium-term consequences (career, finances, relationships); 10 years captures whether it matters at all in the arc of your life. Most heated decisions look very different across these three lenses, and the discrepancy reveals what's actually at stake.
entries.example: Sending an angry email to a colleague: 10 min — cathartic; 10 months — awkward 1:1s and a damaged reference; 10 years — possibly a closed door at a future company. Or: skipping a friend's wedding to finish a deck. 10 min — relief; 10 months — strained friendship; 10 years — you'll remember the wedding, not the deck.
entries.howToApply: When you feel a decision pulling on you emotionally, literally write three lines on paper labeled 10m / 10mo / 10yr and answer each. If the 10-year answer is 'won't matter,' stop overthinking. If 10-month and 10-year answers conflict with the 10-minute pull, the 10-minute pull is almost always the one to discount.
entries.pitfalls: Long horizons can rationalize chronic self-denial ('it won't matter in 10 years' applied to every joy). Some decisions genuinely are about the next 10 minutes (acute pain, safety) and the long view distorts them. The framework is folk wisdom, not validated psychology — treat it as a prompt for reflection, not a proof.
entries.origin: Suzy Welch, '10-10-10: A Fast and Powerful Way to Get Unstuck in Love, at Work, and with Your Family' (Scribner, 2009); Welch first wrote about it in O, The Oprah Magazine in 2006.

entries.name: Bezos Regret-Minimization Framework
entries.oneLiner: When facing a major decision, project yourself to age 80 and choose the option you'll regret least from that vantage point.
entries.description: Jeff Bezos described leaving his Wall Street job in 1994 to start Amazon by mentally fast-forwarding to age 80 and asking which choice would minimize lifetime regret. He realized he wouldn't regret trying and failing at an internet bookstore, but would regret never having tried. The framework reframes risk: short-term loss aversion (giving up a bonus, a title, comfort) shrinks against the asymmetric long-term regret of inaction. It's a practical application of Kahneman's 'experienced self vs. remembering self' distinction.
